summary: For ages 10–11 (UK DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans', statutory requirement to 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'): the whole value of this topic is INTEGRATING two systems the child has met separately — digestion (breaks food into nutrients) and circulation (carries them). The organising idea is a delivery network: food is digested → nutrients and most water are absorbed into the blood at the small-intestine wall (the large intestine absorbs some more water) → the heart pumps blood through vessels → nutrients, water and oxygen are delivered to every cell, and waste is carried away. The key conceptual move is that nutrients do not stay in the gut — they travel in the blood to where they are needed. Keep it at whole-system level (absorb→carry→deliver); capillary diffusion and active transport are KS3.
misconceptions: Thinking nutrients stay in the stomach or gut, rather than being absorbed into the blood and delivered around the body.
Treating digestion and circulation as unrelated systems, missing that circulation delivers what digestion releases.
Believing blood only carries oxygen, overlooking nutrients and water as cargo.
Assuming food 'becomes energy' directly in the gut, skipping the transport of nutrients to cells that then use them.
Thinking transport is one-way (delivery only), missing that blood also carries waste away from cells.

activities.title: Follow one nutrient from a meal to a working cell
steps: Pick a mouthful of food and trace what happens to it as it is digested along the gut.
At the small-intestine wall, identify the pivotal moment: the nutrient crosses OUT of the gut tube and INTO a blood vessel (absorption).
Follow the nutrient as the heart pumps blood carrying it through the vessels out to a working muscle cell (e.g. a leg muscle) that grabs and uses it.
Note the co-passengers — water and oxygen riding along in the blood too — and the waste picked up for the return trip, so blood is understood as two-way transport.
Name each hand-off aloud or in writing: digested in the gut → absorbed into blood at the small intestine → carried by the circulatory system → delivered to the cell.
activities.insight: The digestive and circulatory systems the child learned separately are one connected delivery network: the food you eat is absorbed into the blood and travels to every cell in your body.

activities.title: Trace the journey on a body outline
steps: On a body outline, draw a meal in the gut and a target muscle (e.g. in the leg or toes).
Use a finger or a drawn/coloured line to trace the path from the drawn meal, through the gut, across the small-intestine wall into a blood vessel, through the pumping heart, and out to the muscle.
Narrate each hand-off between systems as you go ('here it's absorbed into the blood', 'here the heart pumps it on', 'here the cell uses it').
Add arrows showing waste returning from the cell back into the blood to show two-way transport.
activities.insight: Drawing and narrating the whole path on a body makes the delivery network a route the learner can reconstruct and explain, not just recognise.

activities.title: Explain the diagnostic 'how do nutrients reach a leg muscle?' question
steps: Consider: after you digest your dinner, nutrients need to reach a muscle in your leg. A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and straight into the leg.
Explain how the nutrients actually get from gut to leg muscle: what carries them, and where do they cross over?

Answer the probing follow-ups: At which organ do nutrients pass out of the gut into the blood? Why does it help that the small intestine has a huge, folded inner surface? If the circulatory system stopped, why would a leg muscle starve even though there's food in the gut? How do the digestive and circulatory systems depend on each other to nourish a cell?
activities.insight: A learner who understands transport routes nutrients via absorption into the blood; one without it imagines food travelling bodily through the gut to its destination, with no role for blood.

checkQuestion: After you digest your dinner, the nutrients need to reach a muscle in your leg. A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and somehow straight into the leg. How do the nutrients actually get from your gut to a leg muscle — what carries them, and where do they cross over?
checkAnswer: The digested nutrients are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; the circulatory system then carries the dissolved nutrients in the blood to every cell, including the leg muscle. The digestive and circulatory systems work together — the gut absorbs, the blood transports.
